title: The Castaway
short: Cowper's last original poem (1799), based on an episode in Anson's Voyage Round the World; published posthumously by Hayley (1803).
body: Cowper wrote the poem in 1799, a year before his death, during his final depression at East Dereham, Norfolk; the exact day is variously given, March or April 1799. He had reread A Voyage Round the World (1748), the official account of Commodore George Anson's circumnavigation of 1740-44, in which a seaman is washed overboard in a storm and watched by his shipmates as he swims until he drowns. William Hayley printed the poem in his Life and Posthumous Writings of William Cowper (1803-04). 'Involved' keeps its Latin sense, wrapped or enveloped (involvere). The poem turns a seaman's death into an image of Cowper's own conviction that he was damned.

title: castaway (title)
short: The title echoes St Paul's fear that he might himself be 'a castaway' (1 Corinthians 9:27), rejected by God: the theological key to the poem.
body: In the King James Bible Paul says he keeps his body under 'lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway' (1 Cor. 9:27; Greek adokimos, 'disapproved, rejected'). For an evangelical reader like Cowper the word meant one finally rejected from salvation. The seaman is literally cast away, an 'outcast' left behind by the ship; Cowper is the spiritual castaway. Cowper had described himself as such years before, and the double sense governs the turn in the last stanza.

anchor: such a destined wretch as I
title: a destined wretch as I
short: 'Destined' carries Calvinist predestination: Cowper believed himself foreordained to damnation, and links himself to the drowning man from the start.
body: Cowper, an evangelical Calvinist, had a dream in 1773 after which he believed he was singled out for damnation, and in 'Lines Written during a Period of Insanity' (c. 1774) he called himself damned below Judas. The comparison 'such ... as I' is placed early, though the poem only explains it in the last stanza; the third line thus quietly frames the narrative as autobiography. Critics debate whether the poem is pure despair or achieves, through the control of its art, a measure of consolation; the startling candour of 'destined' supports the darker reading.

anchor: His floating home for ever left
title: stanza form
short: Eleven six-line stanzas rhyming ababcc, alternating tetrameter and trimeter, then a closing tetrameter couplet: a ballad-like stanza with a sententious close.
body: The first four lines alternate eight and six syllables (common metre, the measure of hymns, including Cowper's own Olney Hymns) and the couplet of two tetrameters gives each stanza a firm, often aphoristic close ('But waged with death a lasting strife, / Supported by despair of life'). The plain hymn metre is part of the poem's terrible irony: the form of congregational faith carries the experience of abandonment by God.

anchor: No braver chief could Albion boast
title: chief ... Albion
short: The 'chief' is Commodore George Anson (1697-1762), whose squadron left England in 1740 against Spanish possessions in the Pacific; Albion is England.
body: Anson's expedition (1740-44), sent out in the War of Jenkins' Ear, lost most of its men to scurvy and storms but captured a Spanish treasure galleon and completed a circumnavigation in the Centurion; Anson later became First Lord of the Admiralty. 'Albion' is the ancient poetic name for Britain. 'He loved them both' means the seaman loved his commander and his country, and 'both in vain' because he never saw either again.

title: whelming brine
short: Overwhelming, engulfing sea; 'whelm' means to cover over or submerge.
body: 'Whelm' (to turn a vessel upside down over something, to engulf) is older than 'overwhelm'. 'Brine' is poetic diction for the sea. The word returns in the last line ('whelm'd in deeper gulfs'), binding the seaman's fate to the poet's. The stanza praises the man's skill and courage ('Expert to swim'), which only prolongs his ordeal. The negatives ('Not long ... Nor soon') stress how slowly his strength fails, so that his drowning is drawn out, not sudden.

title: Supported by despair of life
short: A paradox: despair of surviving keeps him fighting; the line has been read as heroic defiance or as an image of Cowper's own sustaining hopelessness.
body: Literally, knowing he must die, the seaman fights all the harder, a desperate courage. Vincent Newey reads the drowned mariner as a dark double for Cowper's own affliction, and the phrase fits Cowper's own long life sustained in spite of, or by, despair. The antithesis of 'waged with death a lasting strife' and 'despair' sets up the poem's movement from heroic struggle to submersion.

title: pitiless perforce
short: The crew were made pitiless by necessity: the gale gave them no choice but to sail on.
body: 'Perforce' means of necessity, by force of circumstances. In Anson's narrative the ship could not be brought round in the storm. Cowper is fair to the crew: they are 'pitiless' only in effect, not in feeling. 'Scudded' is a sailor's term for running before a gale with little or no sail; Anson's account describes the ship lying-to and then driven. The stanza introduces the poem's ethical complexity: abandonment that no one could prevent.

title: The cask, the coop, the floated cord
short: The crew threw what floats: an empty cask, a hen-coop, a rope paid out on the water, all useless.
body: Ships carried live poultry in wooden coops on deck; coops and empty casks were standard improvised life-buoys. A 'floated cord' is a line let out in the hope the swimmer could reach it. The alliterating list (cask, coop, cord) is precise, in keeping with Cowper's documentary source. The couplet sets the futility plainly: 'nor ship nor shore ... should visit more'.

title: Nor ... could he / Their haste himself condemn
short: The drowning man understands that only flight could save the ship; he does not blame his comrades, yet finds it bitter to die with friends so near.
body: This stanza, Cowper's addition to Anson, gives the seaman an inner life of fairness and grief. Read theologically, it suggests Cowper's refusal to accuse God or the community of believers who could not save him. The final couplet ('bitter ... to die / Deserted, and his friends so nigh') makes nearness the cruelty: the companions are visible but cannot help.

title: self-upheld
short: Keeping himself afloat by his own strength; an hour in such a sea is a long life ('He long survives, who lives an hour').
body: The aphorism compresses Anson's observation that the man swam strongly and long. 'Self-upheld' stresses lonely effort: no other support is available, natural or divine. The stanza's last couplet gives the man's two cries, an appeal and a farewell ('Adieu!'), as if he passes from hope to acceptance. 'Destiny repell'd' returns to the poem's language of fate. For a moment the swimmer seems to hold off what is 'destined', the word Cowper had applied to himself in l. 3.

title: he drank / The stifling wave, and then he sank
short: The narrative ends in a flat, monosyllabic couplet; the internal echo 'drank / sank' enacts the swallowing.
body: The plainness is deliberate: no image or consolation, only physical fact ('toil subdued' him). The comrades 'could catch the sound no more': the sound of his voice in 'every blast' has stopped. The repetition of 'and then' gives the couplet the bare sequence of a log entry, close to the source's matter-of-fact prose. After this point the poem leaves narrative for reflection, so the sinking marks the hinge of its structure.

title: the page / Of narrative sincere ... Anson's tear
short: No poet mourned the seaman, but the published account of the voyage does; the 'tear' is the narrative's expression of regret.
body: The Voyage, though issued under Anson's authority, was compiled by the chaplain Richard Walter and, largely, the mathematician Benjamin Robins; Cowper treats it as Anson's 'narrative sincere', and imagines its page wet with the commander's tear. The stanza's maxim ('tears by bards or heroes shed / Alike immortalize the dead') places the prose of a hero beside poetry as memorial. Kinsley locates the poem within the eighteenth-century voyage-account tradition of maritime suffering.

title: Descanting
short: Discoursing at length, with a musical overtone (a descant is a melody sung over a theme): Cowper disclaims any aim to make the man's fate more lasting.
body: 'Descant' meant first a melodic counterpoint and then, by extension, to comment or enlarge upon a theme (OED). The stanza is a formal disclaimer: the poet does not purpose (intend) to immortalise the man ('A more enduring date'), which the Voyage has done. Instead the motive is psychological: misery likes to see its likeness in another's case. This inverts Lucretius' famous claim (De Rerum Natura 2.1-4) that it is sweet to watch from shore another's struggles at sea: here the watcher is himself drowning.

anchor: No voice divine the storm allay'd
title: No voice divine the storm allay'd
short: Alludes to Christ stilling the storm on the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 8:23-26; Mark 4:39); for the speaker no such miracle came.
body: In the Gospels, when the disciples fear drowning Jesus rebukes the wind and sea, 'and there was a great calm'. Cowper denies the miracle twice: no voice, no 'light propitious' (a favouring light, perhaps a guiding star or the light of grace). The first-person plural 'We perish'd, each alone' joins seaman and poet, and the paradox of a shared solitude is the poem's most quoted line. Virginia Woolf's Mr Ramsay recites it repeatedly in To the Lighthouse (1927), a sign of its later fame.

anchor: But I beneath a rougher sea
title: a rougher sea ... deeper gulfs
short: The final comparison: the poet's spiritual drowning is worse than the seaman's death, a sea of despair and abandonment by God.
body: The closing couplet makes explicit the identity hinted at in 'such a destined wretch as I'. The language recalls the Psalms of the drowning soul ('Deep calleth unto deep ... all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me', Psalm 42:7; 'I am come into deep waters', Psalm 69:2) and Jonah's cry from the deep (Jonah 2:3). 'Gulfs' means abysses. RPO's note recalls that Cowper had described himself in 1773 as a castaway, condemned. Critics differ over whether the final assertion is unrelieved despair or a last act of articulate self-possession; the poem's formal control is often adduced for the second view.
